title: Examining Student and AI Generated Personalized Analogies in Introductory Physics
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether introductory physics students spontaneously use analogies when explaining a complex concept—the Morse potential curve—and how those explanations compare with analogies generated by generative AI. The authors are motivated by prior research suggesting that self-generated analogies can support learning more effectively than instructor-provided ones, but that facilitating personalized analogy generation is difficult in large-enrollment courses. The study asks three main questions: how student and AI explanations differ when describing the curve for second graders, to what extent students can generate analogies in their own preferred everyday contexts, and what students perceive as making the process easy or difficult.

The approach was an online extra-credit activity in which students first explained the Morse potential curve in their own words, then explained it for a second-grade audience, and then explained it using a personally chosen everyday context. In a second phase, students used generative AI to produce comparable explanations and then compared their own and the AI-generated outputs. The analysis combined quantitative coding of hundreds of responses with qualitative thematic analysis of students’ explanations and reflections. The authors analyzed 839 complete responses, representing roughly 800 student submissions, and also examined the AI outputs students generated via prompting.

The participants were students in a first-semester calculus-based introductory physics course for future engineers at a large U.S. Midwestern land-grant university. Data were collected in Spring 2024 during week 11 of the semester, after students had been taught the Morse potential curve. The course was a large-enrollment undergraduate setting, and the activity was delivered online via Qualtrics as an extra-credit assignment expected to take about 60 minutes.

The main findings were that students rarely used spontaneous analogies when asked to explain the curve to second graders, whereas AI outputs used analogies in nearly all such responses. However, when students were explicitly asked to explain the concept in a preferred everyday domain, they overwhelmingly produced analogies and did so across a highly diverse set of contexts. Students reported more difficulty explaining the concept to second graders than explaining it through their own chosen contexts. The authors conclude that AI may help surface personalized analogical possibilities, but that explicit prompting and learner agency are important for eliciting students’ own analogical reasoning. The study also suggests that analogy generation can reveal gaps in students’ conceptual understanding.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: A generative AI chatbot based on large language models that produces human-like text responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used ChatGPT to generate explanations/analogies for the Morse potential curve, especially explanations suitable for second graders, and these AI-generated responses were compared qualitatively with student-generated explanations.

findings.finding_summary: In this qualitative comparison study, AI-generated responses used analogies far more often than student-generated spontaneous explanations to second graders: 806 of 839 AI responses (96%) contained analogies, compared with 323 of 839 student responses using analogies and 501 of 839 student responses (60%) using no comparisons. The paper interprets this as showing potential for AI to facilitate personalized analogical reasoning, while also noting that AI responses differed qualitatively from students’ own spontaneous reasoning and were sometimes affected by improper prompting.
findings.measure: Presence and type of comparisons (analogy/similarity/neither) in explanations of the Morse potential curve for second graders

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical qualitative study with a large course sample, but it does not use an experimental causal design to estimate learning effects of the AI tool on student outcomes. Findings are based on coded response patterns rather than validated outcome gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear qualitative differences in AI versus student analogy generation, but it does not report effect sizes or direct learning gains attributable to ChatGPT. Impact on student learning is therefore promising but unclear.
